idiom_name: error-first guards: if err != nil { return err }
implementation_notes: Go's multiple return values and the error interface make the guard the default statement: each fallible call is followed by if err != nil and the guard returns the zero value plus the error, so the happy path runs at the top indentation level. What replaces the classic wrapped conditional is the language convention itself - the Go blog shows the shape and the appHandler refactor that removes repeated handling - and the same shape appears as continue in loops, where it filters an item without indenting the processing body. panic is reserved for impossible states and must-style constructors; anything a caller can cause exits with an error.
pitfalls: Returning a non-nil value together with an error (or a nil error beside a zero value) breaks the convention every caller tests; on failure return the zero value and the error.
Shadowing err with := inside an if block keeps the outer error nil; be sure which error the caller finally sees.
Discarding an error with _ or logging and continuing turns failure into a silent default; wrap it with %w and return it.
